title: Ang 818–830: Guru Arjan's shelter
hookLine: no hot wind touches, on ang 819
tomorrow: who helps when the people who love you can't?

cards: A heat advisory pops up on the phone: stay inside, drink water, check on older neighbors. On ang 819, Guru Arjan uses a day like that as his picture. The hot wind, he says, doesn't touch the one in God's shelter.
Families still sing this hymn when someone they love is sick. So what does it promise, and what doesn't it?

teach.h: NO HOT WIND IN HIS SHELTER.
teach.b: In paraphrase, the hymn on ang 819: the hot wind does not touch the one in the Supreme Lord's shelter.
All around us the Lord has drawn his line; pain can't get in, brother.

I met the perfect True Guru, who made it so, and he gave the medicine of the Name. Then the close: the Protector protected, the sickness was taken away; says Nanak, grace came, and God became our help.

That line all around is kaar, a mark drawn on the ground to protect what's inside it. Tradition ties this hymn to the young Hargobind, Guru Arjan's son and the sixth Guru to come, getting well from an illness.
So hear it twice. Once as thanks: someone was sick, and they recovered. And once as a picture for anyone: a circle drawn by God, not by you.
Here's the honest part. The hymn doesn't say there's no heat. It was sung after a fever, by people who knew fevers.
It says the heat doesn't get through the line. And notice it still talks about medicine.
Shelter and care go together in this hymn; trusting God and calling the doctor aren't rivals.
That's Guru Arjan's shelter: a line drawn all the way around, and a hot wind blowing outside it.

how: Sikh families and sangats often sing 'taatee vaao na lagaee' (ang 819) as a shabad of protection and thanks, especially when someone is ill or has recovered.

games.q: your neighbor's little boy has a high fever. his mom is reciting a prayer while she waits for the doctor to call back, and asks you to sit with her. what fits ang 819?
o: sit with her and help her keep calling; shelter and care belong together.
tell her the prayer is enough, so she can stop worrying about the doctor.
tell her worrying changes nothing, and she should try to get some rest.
games.why: Guru Arjan's hymn names both the shelter and the medicine. trust and care aren't rivals here.

practice: Put both palms flat on something solid: the floor, a table, a wall. Feel how it holds you up without asking anything back. Rest there for the sit, and if someone you love is unwell, keep them inside that circle with you.
If you'd like, read the hymn on ang 819 first.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sarnai, shelter, sanctuary; 'paarbraham sarnaaee', ang 819.

carryVoice: Sheltered: the heat still blows, and the line around you holds. That's the hymn after the fever.
